bai.moTa: Today’s actual positions; the Sun travels at 828,000 km/h
bai.yChinh: Eight planets orbit the Sun, and the Sun itself is in motion. It carries its whole family around the center of the Milky Way at **828,000 km/h**. Seen from the Galaxy, each planet traces a helix. Observers see different shapes for the very same motion: the shape of a path depends on the observer’s frame of reference.
bai.giaiThich:
The model shows the planets’ **actual positions today**, calculated from NASA/JPL orbital tables. Distances are to scale. The planets and the Sun are enlarged so you can see them.

Seen from the Galaxy, the Sun travels at 230 km/s toward the constellation Cygnus. The orbital plane makes an angle of about **60°** with the direction of travel, so each planet’s path resembles a spring stretched at a slant. At true scale the spring is greatly stretched: each year the Sun travels 48.5 AU while Earth completes an orbit only 6.28 AU long. By default the model **compresses the Sun’s path by a factor of 10**.

There is no absolutely stationary viewpoint. To describe an object’s motion, you have to say what it is moving relative to.
bai.conSo.1: **828,000 km/h** (230 km/s): the Sun’s speed around the center of the Galaxy. Measurements give values between 220 and 250 km/s.
bai.conSo.2: **48.5 AU per year**: the distance the Sun travels, nearly 8 times the length of Earth’s orbit (6.28 AU).
bai.conSo.3: **8.3 minutes**: the time light takes to travel 1 AU = 149.6 million km. It takes 4.2 hours to reach Neptune.
bai.conSo.4: **$T^2 = a^3$**: Kepler’s third law (years, AU), accurate to within 0.2% for all eight planets.
bai.conSo.5: **172 AU ≈ one light-day**: the distance Voyager 1 has reached after 49 years of flight. Traveling the distance to the nearest star would take about another 75,000 years.
bai.conSo.6: **About 220 million years**: one galactic year. The Sun has completed only about 20 orbits.
bai.hieuDung: **The planets do not form a vortex.** Some online videos show the planets spiraling into a funnel trailing the Sun. Two features are wrong: planets can be ahead of the Sun or behind it, and their orbital plane makes an angle of about 60° with its direction of travel, rather than a right angle.
bai.nguon: NASA/JPL approximate planetary orbits (Standish and Williams, 1800–2050). JPL Horizons: positions and velocities of Voyager 1 and 2 on 11/11/2026. Planetary rotation axes and rotation rates: IAU WGCCRE (Archinal et al., 2018). Planetary radii: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet. Dates and distances at which the Voyagers left the heliosphere: NASA/JPL (2012, 2018). Proxima Centauri lies 4.25 light-years away. The Sun’s speed and R₀: measured speeds of 220–250 km/s; the GRAVITY Collaboration (2019–2021) gives R₀ ≈ 8.2 kpc. Constants: CODATA 2018, IAU 2012.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: Describe the Solar System’s motion relative to the Milky Way and state its speed.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Picture the true scale of the Solar System using astronomical units and light-travel times.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Use Kepler’s third law, $T^2 = a^3$, to calculate an orbital period from distance, and derive the law from Newton’s law of gravitation.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Explain why, as seen from the Galaxy, the planets trace slanting helices rather than a swirling funnel.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.5: Calculate a galactic year from the Sun’s orbital radius and speed.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
Here is the Solar System as seen from the Milky Way. The bright sphere is the Sun. It races toward the constellation Cygnus at about **230 km/s**, carrying all eight planets with it. Each bright trail shows where a planet has traveled over the past few decades. As the planet orbits, the Sun carries it forward, so the trail forms a **helix**.

- The tightest coils, close to the Sun, belong to Mercury and Venus.
- The blue trail is Earth’s. Each turn represents one year.
- The much wider, more widely spaced coils belong to Jupiter and Saturn.

> [Con số] $230\ \text{km/s} \times 3\,600\ \text{s} = 828\,000$ km per hour. In the few seconds it takes you to read this sentence, the entire Solar System travels more than 1,000 km.

> [Lưu ý] The Sun’s path is drawn **10 times shorter** to make the coils visible. The Sun and planets are drawn much larger than their actual sizes. Steps 3 and 6 explain the true scale.

> [Thử ngay] Drag to rotate and scroll to zoom. Hover over a planet to see its actual data, or click it to fly closer.
> [[View from the front|truoc]] [[Side view|dau]] [[Observe from the Sun|quay]]

The same motion can trace entirely different shapes when seen from two different places. That is the idea we will follow through this lesson.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.de: Rotate the view to look **along the direction of travel**, from ahead of the Sun or behind it. Make the yellow arrow point straight toward you or straight away. The Sun’s forward motion then disappears from view, and each helix collapses into a set of nested closed loops. The challenge is complete when your viewing direction is within 6° of the line of travel.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.goiY: Click “View from the front” to get close, then drag the mouse very slowly. Each loop is an orbit seen at an angle, so it looks a little flattened (its axes are in a ratio of about 0.86 because the orbital plane is at 60° to the direction of travel). Perspective makes the more distant loops look smaller.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.ten: Seen from the Sun: the eight planets today
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Now we are at rest relative to the Sun, as in a familiar textbook illustration. Each planet moves along a nearly circular ellipse. The bright tail shows the part of its orbit it has just traveled.

These are the planets’ **actual positions today**, calculated from NASA/JPL’s approximate orbital tables. The tables give six numbers for each planet, including the {{bán trục lớn|semi-major axis}}, eccentricity, and inclination, together with their rates of change per century. The computer then solves Kepler’s equation to find a position on any date from 1800 to 2050. The result differs from a precise ephemeris by about a few arcminutes.

- The four inner rocky planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.
- The asteroid belt: 2.1–3.3 AU.
- The four giant planets: Jupiter and Saturn (gas giants), Uranus and Neptune (ice giants).
- The Kuiper belt: 30–50 AU, home to Pluto.

> [Lưu ý] A few thousand dots in the two belts **illustrate the distribution**. The real belts contain many more objects. Individual dots do not correspond to specific real objects.

> [Thử ngay] Hover over a planet to see its data. Click its name to pin the data in the controls. Drag Earth (the blue dot) along its orbit to move time forward or backward. All the planets move to their positions on that date.
> [[See all eight planets|ngoai]] [[Return to the inner orbits|trong]] [[Earth data|dat]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.de: Drag Earth to the day it **overtakes Mars**, when the Sun, Earth, and Mars line up. Mars is then at opposition, close to us and at its brightest. Complete the challenge by bringing the planets within 1.5° of each other as seen from the Sun.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.goiY: Earth travels faster on its inner orbit, so it catches up with Mars. Drag Earth forward about a quarter of an orbit. The next opposition falls around 02/20/2027.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.ten: True scale: a vast expanse of empty space
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
In the model, **distances are to scale**, while **sizes are enlarged**. At true scale Earth would be smaller than a pixel. Imagine shrinking everything until the Sun is a ball 1.4 m in diameter:

| Object | Actual | Scale model |
|---|---|---|
| Sun | diameter 1,391,400 km | a ball 1.4 m across |
| Earth | diameter 12,742 km, distance 1 AU | a marble 1.3 cm across, 150 m away |
| Jupiter | diameter 139,822 km, distance 5.2 AU | an orange 14 cm across, 780 m away |
| Neptune | 30 AU away | 4.5 km away |
| Voyager 1 | 172 AU away | 26 km away |
| Nearest star | 4.25 light-years | 40,000 km away |

On this scale, the distance to the nearest star is about one trip around the real Earth.

An {{Đơn vị thiên văn|astronomical unit}} (AU) is the mean Earth–Sun distance, 149.6 million km. Light takes 499 seconds to travel 1 AU, so that distance is **8.3 light-minutes**. Jupiter is about 43 light-minutes from the Sun, and Neptune is 4.2 light-hours away.

> [Lưu ý] The Sun is drawn at least 7 times its actual size. Planets are enlarged by factors ranging from about 80 for Jupiter to nearly 600 for Mercury; Earth is enlarged about 330 times. They are magnified further as you zoom out so that each stays at least a few pixels across. Surface markings help you recognize the planets. Earth’s coastlines follow the real coastlines; the other markings are illustrations.

> [Thử ngay] The thin circles form a distance ruler that also shows light-travel time. Fly closer with the buttons below or click a planet. Time then slows to 1 hour per second, so you can see the planet rotate:
> [[Earth|dat]] [[Jupiter|moc]] [[Saturn|tho]] [[Sun|mt]] [[Return to the full view|toan]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
The farther a planet is from the Sun, the slower it moves and the longer its orbit. Johannes Kepler found the precise laws from Tycho Brahe’s observations and published them in 1609 and 1619:

1. Each planet moves on an **ellipse**, with the Sun at one focus.
2. The line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times: the planet moves faster near the Sun and more slowly farther away.
3. The square of the period $T$ is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis $a$ (half the long axis of the ellipse):

$$ T^2 = a^3 \qquad (T \text{ in years},\ a \text{ in AU}) $$

| Planet | $a$ (AU) | $T$ (years) | $T^2/a^3$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mercury | 0.387 | 0.241 | 1.000 |
| Venus | 0.723 | 0.615 | 1.000 |
| Earth | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 |
| Mars | 1.524 | 1.881 | 1.000 |
| Jupiter | 5.203 | 11.86 | 0.999 |
| Saturn | 9.537 | 29.45 | 1.000 |
| Uranus | 19.19 | 84.02 | 0.999 |
| Neptune | 30.07 | 164.8 | 0.999 |

The table uses the model’s own data. The graph in the controls plots $T$ against $a$ on logarithmic axes. The eight points lie on a straight line with slope 3/2.

> [Ví dụ] For Jupiter, $T = 5{,}203^{1,5} \approx 11{,}87$ years, in agreement with the 11.86 years in the table.

+++ Go deeper: deriving the third law from Newton’s law
Consider a circular orbit of radius $r$ and speed $v$. The gravitational force from the Sun, of mass $M$, provides the centripetal force:

$$ \frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{m v^2}{r} $$

Substitute $v = 2\pi r / T$ and simplify:

$$ T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}\, r^3 $$

The planet’s mass $m$ cancels, so all the planets share the same constant $4\pi^2/GM$. In years and AU, the Sun’s $GM$ is approximately $4\pi^2$ (within 0.004%), so $T^2 = a^3$. For an elliptical orbit, replace the radius $r$ by the semi-major axis $a$.

The ratios in the table differ from 1 by less than 0.2% because the planets also pull on the Sun (Jupiter has about 1/1,047 of the Sun’s mass), and they pull on one another.
+++

> [Lưu ý] Listen to the model: each planet sounds a note when it completes an orbit, so the time between notes is the period $T$. Pitch reflects orbital speed at 22 Hz per km/s. Mercury (47 km/s) has the highest pitch and Neptune (5.4 km/s) the lowest. This converts speed to something we can hear; the planets do not make these sounds.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the test planet (the pink dot) toward or away from the Sun. Its period changes according to $T = a^{1,5}$, and its pitch drops as it moves farther out.
> [[10 years per second|nhanh]] [[1 month per second|cham]] [[View the inner orbits|trong]] [[View all eight planets|ngoai]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Place the test planet where one orbit around the Sun takes exactly **8 years**. The challenge is complete when the difference is less than 0.25 years.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: If $T = 8$, then $a^3 = T^2 = 64$, so $a = 4$ AU, between Mars and Jupiter. The label beside the test planet shows $a$ and $T$.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.ten: Why a helix? Adding two velocities
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Seen from the Galaxy, each planet’s velocity is the **sum** of two parts:

$$ \vec v_{\text{planet}} = \vec V_{\text{Sun}} + \vec v_{\text{orbit}} $$

- $\vec V$ is the same for all planets: 230 km/s toward Cygnus (the yellow arrow).
- $\vec v_{\text{orbit}}$ follows the planet’s orbit. For Earth its magnitude is 29.8 km/s.

Adding uniform straight-line motion to circular motion produces a helix. The orbital plane (the faint blue disk) makes an angle of **about 60°** with the direction of travel, so $\vec V$ has two components:

- Perpendicular to the orbital plane: $230 \times \sin 60° \approx 200$ km/s, stretching the circle into a spring.
- In the plane: $230 \times \cos 60° \approx 115$ km/s, pushing the coils **to one side**.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] In some online videos the Sun looks like a comet with its planets spiraling into a funnel behind it. Two features are wrong. The planets sometimes lead the Sun and sometimes trail it. Their orbital plane is also inclined to the direction of travel, rather than perpendicular to it.

+++ Go deeper: Earth’s actual speed relative to the galactic center
Let $\alpha \approx 60°$ be the angle between the direction of travel and the orbital plane, and let $\varphi$ give Earth’s position in its orbit. The component of $\vec v_{\text{orbit}}$ along the direction of travel equals $v \cos\alpha \cos\varphi$, so

$$ |\vec v_{\text{planet}}| = \sqrt{V^2 + v^2 + 2Vv\cos\alpha\cos\varphi} $$

Substitute $V = 230$, $v = 29{,}8$ km/s, and $\cos\alpha \approx 0{,}5$. The maximum is about 246 km/s and the minimum about 216 km/s. Over the year Earth is alternately faster and slower than the Sun by about 15 km/s.
+++

> [Thử ngay] [[View from the front|truoc]] [[Side view|ngang]] [[Look along the orbital plane|phang]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Each year Earth completes an orbit $2\pi \times 1\ \text{AU} \approx 6{,}28$ AU long. In that same year the Sun travels

$$ \begin{aligned} 230\ \text{km/s} \times 3{,}156 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s} &\approx 7{,}26 \times 10^{9}\ \text{km} \\ &\approx 48{,}5\ \text{AU} \end{aligned} $$

So the pitch of the actual helix is nearly **8 times** the circumference of a coil. It is so stretched that it looks like an almost straight line with a slight wave. The effect is even more pronounced for Neptune. One orbit takes 165 years, during which the Sun travels nearly 8,000 AU, while Neptune’s orbital circumference is only 189 AU.

By default the model therefore **shortens the Sun’s path by a factor of 10**. The pitch of Earth’s helix drops to 4.85 AU and the coils become clear.

> [Thử ngay] [[True scale|that]] [[Compress by a factor of 10|nen]]

> [Con số] Lesson 4 builds a different helix: Earth’s world line in spacetime. Its pitch is **one light-year**, or 63,241 AU, about 1,300 times the 48.5 AU pitch here. This lesson’s helix lies in space and appears when we observe from the Galaxy. The helix in Lesson 4 lies in spacetime and is there for every observer.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.ten: Voyager: half a century to travel one light-day
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
The two Voyagers left Earth in 1977 and flew past Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 2 also visited Uranus and Neptune. Gravity from these planets slung the spacecraft out of the Solar System. The positions and velocities shown here come from JPL Horizons.

- **Voyager 1** is traveling at 16.9 km/s, moving 3.57 AU farther away each year. It is now about 172 AU from the Sun, or 0.995 **light-days**. It will be exactly one light-day away around early February 2027.
- **Voyager 2** is traveling at 15.3 km/s and is now about 144 AU away.

The faint sphere of radius 120 AU represents the {{nhật quyển|heliosphere}}, the region reached by the solar wind before it encounters interstellar gas. Voyager 1 crossed its boundary in August 2012 at 121 AU; Voyager 2 crossed in November 2018 at 119 AU. The real heliosphere has a nose and a tail. The sphere here is a schematic.

The nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is 4.25 light-years away. Even at Voyager 1’s speed, covering that distance would take about **75,000 years**, and Voyager 1 is heading in a different direction.

> [Con số] In the 49 years the spacecraft have been flying, the Sun has carried them about 2,400 AU around the Galaxy, 14 times the distance Voyager 1 has traveled under its own motion.

> [Thử ngay] Drag Voyager 1 along its flight path to move through time, starting in 1990.
> [[Rewind to 1990|lui]] [[Return to today|nay]] [[Voyager 1 data|v1]]
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.thuThach.de: Drag Voyager 1 to the moment it is **one light-day** (173.1 AU) from the Sun. Aim to be within 0.6 AU, about two months of travel.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.thuThach.goiY: Voyager 1 gets 3.57 AU farther away each year. It is now about 172 AU away, so advance it just a few months. Scroll to zoom in for a more precise drag.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.ten: A galactic year, and why the shape depends on the observer
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
The Sun does not travel in a straight line forever. It follows a nearly circular orbit around the galactic center with a radius of $R_0 \approx 26\,700$ light-years. One orbit takes

$$ \begin{aligned} T = \frac{2\pi R_0}{V} &= \frac{2\pi \times 26\,700\ \text{light-years}}{230\ \text{km/s}} \\ &\approx 2{,}19 \times 10^{8}\ \text{years} \end{aligned} $$

or about **220 million years**. This is a {{năm thiên hà|galactic year}}. The Sun is 4.6 billion years old, so it has completed only about **20 orbits** (21 using the calculation above). Books often give 225–250 million years, using slightly different measurements of $V$ and $R_0$. Current measurements put $V$ between 220 and 250 km/s.

+++ Go deeper: the calculation step by step
$V/c = 230 / 299\,792 \approx 7{,}67 \times 10^{-4}$: the Sun needs about $1/(7{,}67 \times 10^{-4}) \approx 1\,303$ years to travel one light-year. The circumference of its orbit is $2\pi \times 26\,700 \approx 167\,800$ light-years, so one orbit takes $167\,800 \times 1\,303 \approx 2{,}19 \times 10^{8}$ years.
+++

### What do all observers agree on?
Earth’s motion traces an ellipse when viewed from the Sun, and a skewed helix when viewed from the Galaxy. Watch long enough, and the helix itself winds around the galactic center. Neither view is more correct. Observers agree on **the events**: where Earth is and when. Joining them gives its {{đường thế giới|world line}} in four-dimensional spacetime. Part 2, especially Lesson 4, builds this very line.

> [Thử ngay] [[See all 150 years of the flight path|xa]] [[Return to the opening view|dau]]
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.ten: The Sun’s speed around the galactic center
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.1.y: Measurements give values between 220 and 250 km/s.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: $T$: period; $a$: semi-major axis; $M$: mass of the Sun. The result is independent of the planet’s mass.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.ten: Adding velocities when changing reference frames
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: Galilean velocity addition is an excellent approximation when speeds are small compared with the speed of light.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.5.y: $R_0 \approx 26\,700$ light-years: the Sun’s distance from the galactic center.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: Viewed from the Milky Way, at rest relative to its center, what shape does Earth’s path through space take?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.1: A closed ellipse around the Sun
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.2: A spring that is stretched and skewed
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.chon.3: A swirling funnel trailing the Sun
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: Earth’s velocity combines the 230 km/s motion shared by the whole Solar System with its 29.8 km/s orbital motion. The result looks like a spring. Its coils are skewed because the orbital plane is at 60° to the direction of travel. The ellipse is the view from the Sun. The swirling funnel is the incorrect picture in viral videos.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: Mars has a semi-major axis of 1.524 AU. According to Kepler’s third law, how long does one orbit take?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: $T = a^{1,5} = 1{,}524^{1,5} \approx 1{,}88$ years (687 days). Choosing 1.52 uses $T = a$; 2.32 is $a^2$; 3.54 is $a^3$ (missing the square root).
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: Shrink the Solar System until the Sun is a ball 1.4 m across. How far would Earth be from the ball?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: The scale factor is $1{,}4\ \text{m} / 1\,391\,400\ \text{km}$. Multiplying 149.6 million km by this factor gives about 150 m. Book illustrations usually place planets close to the Sun, so it is easy to underestimate the distance.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: Jupiter is about 5.2 AU from the Sun. How long does sunlight take to reach it?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: Light takes 8.3 minutes per AU, so it takes about 43 minutes to cross 5.2 AU. The 8.3 minutes apply to Earth and 4.2 hours to Neptune. Voyager 1 will soon be one light-day away.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: Why does the model shorten the Sun’s path by a factor of 10 when seen from the Galaxy?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.1: Because the real Sun moves more slowly than the stated speed
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.2: Because each turn advances nearly 8 times the length of Earth’s orbit, making the path look almost straight
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.3: Because the orbital plane is tilted by 60°
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.4: Because light takes time to reach our eyes
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: The Sun travels 48.5 AU per year while Earth completes an orbit only 6.28 AU long. At true scale the coils almost disappear. The factor of 10 changes only the drawing; the actual motion stays the same. Click “True scale” to compare.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: You are sitting still on a chair. Are you moving or at rest? Give a precise answer and identify something all observers agree on.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: The question needs a **reference frame**. Relative to the chair you are at rest. Relative to the Sun you are moving at 29.8 km/s (plus a few hundred m/s from Earth’s rotation). Relative to the galactic center your speed is about 230 km/s. There is no absolutely stationary viewpoint. Everyone agrees on the **events**, such as “I am sitting on this chair at 9 o’clock,” and on the world line connecting them in spacetime.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: A. Einstein, *Relativity: The Special and the General Theory* (1916), opening sections: reference frames and the relativity of motion, illustrated by a stone dropped from a railway carriage.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: E. F. Taylor and J. A. Wheeler, *Spacetime Physics* (2nd edition, 1992), ch. 3: the principle of relativity and the absence of absolute motion.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), ch. 10: the Solar System as a laboratory for testing general relativity. Lesson 13 returns to this topic.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: Half the longest diameter of an elliptical orbit. It also equals the average of the smallest and largest distances from the Sun. Its symbol is $a$.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: Three laws of planetary motion: elliptical orbits, equal areas swept in equal times, and $T^2$ proportional to $a^3$. Newton derived all three from his law of gravitation.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: The region around the Sun occupied by the solar wind. Its outer boundary, the heliopause, is about 120 AU from the Sun in the direction of the Voyagers’ flight.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: The time the Sun takes to orbit the galactic center, about 220–250 million years depending on the measurements used.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.5.nghia: The object or group of objects chosen as the reference for describing position and motion, as in “relative to the Sun” or “relative to the galactic center.”
